Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
I have always loved the hour before the world wakes. The kitchen is cold and quiet and smelling of rain. Outside the window the street belongs to nobody at all. I make tea slowly because rushing would ruin the moment. Steam rises and curls against the glass like soft smoke. In that silence my thoughts finally learn how to breathe. I think about the lives I might have lived elsewhere. Some were braver and some were kinder and some louder. Yet somehow this small life still feels stubbornly like mine. That feeling is enough to begin almost any hard day.

When I was young I believed wonder lived far away. I imagined it waiting in mountains oceans and bright cities. I saved maps and stories like tickets for someday travel. Now I find wonder hiding much closer to my home. It lives in bread rising warm beside a winter window. It lives in neighbors waving without knowing my whole story. It lives in books reopened after many years of dust. Wonder is not scarce but attention is often too hurried. Slow looking turns ordinary afternoons into something quietly astonishing everywhere. I am still learning how to look without immediately judging.

Memory is a strange and generous and unreliable old friend. It keeps the taste of summer plums from childhood gardens. It forgets appointments but remembers every embarrassment with painful clarity. Sometimes a song unlocks a room I thought was gone. Suddenly I am twelve again and running toward the sea. The air smells of salt and sunscreen and hot sand. My mother calls my name across wind and laughing voices. For one bright instant the past is not past anymore. Then the song ends and ordinary time gently returns again. I am grateful even for that brief impossible visit homeward.

Books have been the most patient teachers I ever had. They waited on shelves while I wasted years being busy. They never scolded me for arriving late to their wisdom. A good novel lets me borrow another persons inner life. For a while I see through eyes unlike my own. That borrowing makes cruelty harder and curiosity much easier daily. Poetry does something else entirely with far fewer words usually. It leaves deliberate spaces where my own feelings can enter. A single image can stay with me for whole decades. I carry lines like smooth stones in my coat pockets.

Friendship at its best feels like a well worn path. You do not need directions and you never perform perfection. Old friends remember versions of you that you have forgotten. They hold those selves kindly until you can reclaim them. Laughter with them has a sound unlike any other laughter. It starts before the joke ends because history is funny. Even silence between friends can feel full rather than empty. Distance weakens some bonds but strangely strengthens a precious few. A letter arriving unexpectedly can repair an entire difficult week. I want to become someone who writes such letters often.

The garden teaches patience in a language without any words. Seeds refuse to hurry however anxiously I watch them daily. Rain arrives or does not arrive despite all my planning. Tomatoes ripen exactly when they are ready and not before. My hands in soil remember something older than my worries. Gardening humbles ambition and rewards simple faithful care every season. A weed is only a plant growing where I disapprove. That definition says more about me than about the weed. Bees go about their business with enviable clarity of purpose. I envy them until I remember humans can choose purpose.

Walking is my favorite way to think without forcing thought. My feet find a rhythm and my mind follows obediently. Problems that seemed enormous indoors shrink under a wide sky. Streets reveal stories when you move slowly enough to notice. An old man waters flowers with ceremonial seriousness every morning. Two children argue passionately about rules they invented seconds ago. A cat watches everyone from a wall like a monarch. Cities are libraries if you know how to read them. Every walk returns me home slightly different from before somehow. Motion reminds me that stagnation is rarely the whole truth.

I have learned to distrust my first reaction during conflict. Anger often arrives dressed as certainty but wearing borrowed clothes. Waiting one night changes many sentences I wanted to send. Kindness is not weakness though frequently mistaken for it today. Courage usually looks quieter than movies have taught us expect. It is apologizing first and listening longer than feels comfortable. It is staying present when leaving would be much easier. Forgiveness does not erase harm but loosens its daily grip. Some apologies arrive too late yet still deserve gentle hearing. Growth is rarely dramatic and almost never conveniently well timed.

Technology has given us miracles and stolen our boredom away. I miss boredom because boredom once invented games and stories. Now every waiting moment begs for a glowing small screen. Still I love hearing distant voices instantly across vast oceans. A photograph can cross the world before breakfast is finished. The tool is neither angel nor demon but a mirror. It shows us what we already hunger for most deeply. Attention may be the purest currency of a human life. Where I spend it shapes who I slowly become eventually. So I try to spend it as deliberately as money.

If I could give advice I would keep it simple. Read widely walk often write honestly and rest without guilt. Tell people you love them before occasions make it easy. Keep one notebook for thoughts too strange for polite company. Plant something living and learn its particular needs with humility. Leave places and people better than you found them today. Expect sorrow but do not let sorrow monopolize the story. Joy will return in unexpected forms if doors stay open. Tonight the tea is warm and the world feels possible. I lift my cup to tomorrow and all its unknowns.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical first-person meditation built from small domestic scenes and reflections on how to live.

## Grounded reading
The voice is calm, intimate, and gently encouraging, finding emotional weight in tea, books, walks, gardens, and old friendships. Its pathos is modest: memory briefly restores the past, conflict tests kindness, and attention helps ordinary life feel meaningful. The reader is invited to slow down, notice more, and practice care without expecting a dramatic cure or revelation.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample repeatedly pairs ordinary objects and routines with moral or emotional lessons: tea with possibility, books with empathy, gardening with patience, walking with perspective, and technology with the stewardship of attention. It foregrounds gentleness, curiosity, forgiveness, friendship, and deliberate living, while allowing sorrow and regret a place without giving them the final word.

## Evidence line
> Attention may be the purest currency of a human life.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sustained attention to ordinary life, patience, and humane conduct gives the sample a coherent sensibility, though its reassuring maxims and familiar lyrical images make that sensibility less distinctive.
